title: Query optimisation: cost estimation
lead: Catalog statistics, selectivity formulas, join cardinality and histograms.

sections.title: Cost and cardinality statistics
sections.html:
From plan operators to estimated total cost

An optimiser needs a closed operator set, alternative physical implementations, a plan space, a cost model and a search procedure. Costing an operator requires input cardinalities; estimating its output cardinality is equally necessary because that output becomes the next operator’s input.

System R combines I/O and CPU work as #I/Os + CPU-factor × #tuples. The factor translates tuple processing into comparable units. Add costs over the actual plan, respecting pipelining and materialisation; do not count an intermediate write if the chosen execution never writes it. A cheaper estimate is a model prediction, not a measured runtime.

PDF pp. 1–3

Catalog statistics and selectivity

NTuples counts rows, NPages counts table/index pages, Low/High bound a column, NKeys counts distinct values and Height describes an index. Catalogs are refreshed periodically or manually, for example by ANALYZE, because exact continuous maintenance is costly. Stale statistics and estimation error are separate sources of poor plans.

For a selection, selectivity = output rows / input rows, between zero and one. Multiply input size by selectivity to estimate output. For a join, start with the product of the two input sizes. “Highly selective” normally means a predicate keeps few rows, hence a small numerical selectivity.

PDF pp. 4–5

sections.title: Predicate selectivity
sections.html:
Equality and range estimates

For a unique key, equality returns at most one row. Under a uniform distribution on V distinct values, sel(A=c)=1/V when c occurs. For integer values spanning L…H, sel(A>a)≈(H−a)/(H−L+1); for a continuous domain, use (H−a)/(H−L). Clamp estimates at domain boundaries and account for whether endpoints are included.

With ages 20…24, age=22 has estimate 1/5 and age>22 keeps ages 23,24, giving 2/5. The integer +1 matters. Gaps and unequal frequencies invalidate a uniform active-domain assumption; NULL handling also needs its own statistics.

PDF pp. 6–7

Matching columns and combining predicates

The estimate sel(A=B)=1/max(VA,VB) assumes independence, uniformity and appropriate overlap. With A taking {v1,v2} equally and B taking {v1,…,v10} equally, only two matching pairs contribute: 2×(1/2×1/10)=1/10. This derives MAX rather than MIN; disjoint domains would instead yield zero.

For two-valued predicates, sel(NOT P)=1−sel(P). Under independence, sel(P AND Q)=sel(P)sel(Q); inclusion–exclusion gives sel(P OR Q)=sel(P)+sel(Q)−sel(P AND Q). Age and department may be correlated, so multiplying their marginal frequencies can fail. In SQL, NOT over a nullable predicate does not count UNKNOWN as TRUE; subtract the NULL fraction where needed.

PDF pp. 8–9

sections.title: Join cardinality
sections.html:
Join cardinalities

If S.A is a non-null foreign key referencing a unique R.A, each S row matches exactly one R row: |R join S|=|S|. Nullable foreign keys can reduce the inner-join result; missing referential integrity removes the guarantee.

For a general equality join, view it as a selection on R×S. The source estimates |R||S|/max(NKeys(R.A),NKeys(S.A)). It takes the smaller of the estimates obtained by treating either side’s values as the matching domain. Repeated values produce many pairs; a join is not generally bounded by either input size. Skew, correlation and partial overlap can strongly change the result.

PDF pp. 10–11

Defaults and the failure of uniformity

Without usable statistics, an optimiser must fall back to constants. The source screenshot is from PostgreSQL 13.0 selfuncs.h and illustrates implementation defaults, not measured properties of a particular table. The next two plots compare a uniform approximation with a non-uniform distribution: equal average frequency hides peaks and valleys, causing different predicates with the same model estimate to have different actual cardinalities.

PDF pp. 12–14

sections.title: Equi-width and equi-depth histograms
sections.html:
Histogram representation

Split the active domain into adjacent buckets (bᵢ₋₁,bᵢ]. Store boundaries, tuple counts and possibly distinct-value counts. Equi-width keeps equal domain width; equi-depth aims for equal tuple counts and changes bucket widths. More buckets improve resolution at a catalog-space and collection cost. Both still approximate the distribution inside each bucket.

PDF pp. 15–16

Equi-width: reconstructing the source calculations

The plotted 16 integer positions have the following frequencies (position 4 has frequency zero; the slide’s “16 distinct values” label counts the displayed domain positions). They sum to 64.

A12345678910111213141516
Frequency1220164889733532

With four buckets, w=(16−1+1)/4=4. Counts for [1,4],[5,8],[9,12],[13,16] are 5,19,27,13. For A=5, distribute the second count uniformly: 19/4=4.75≈5, although the actual frequency is 1. For 7<A≤16, count the last two buckets fully and one quarter of [5,8]: 27+13+19/4=44.75≈45. The actual frequency sum for 8…16 is 48; the example exposes estimation error rather than hiding it.

PDF pp. 17–20

Equi-depth and adaptive resolution

For B=4 and 64 tuples, target depth d=16. The source boundaries give [1,7],[8,9],[10,11],[12,16], each containing 16 tuples. Frequent values receive narrower buckets. In the separate customer-age example, 5,600 tuples and B=8 yield depth 700: the boundaries concentrate around ages 30–59, where observations are dense, rather than assigning the same width to the sparse extremes. Keep these two example populations separate.

PDF pp. 21–23

Estimating inside equi-depth buckets

For A=5, the first bucket spans seven integer positions, so estimate 16/7≈2. For 5<A≤16, count three complete buckets and positions 6,7 in the first: 16+16+16+(2/7)16≈52.57≈53. This differs from the equi-width range example because its lower bound is 5, not 7. The actual result here is 58. Neither histogram makes each estimate exact.

The final recipe is output=input×selectivity, uniformity within each bucket, and independence when combining predicates. General joins multiply Cartesian-product size by estimated join-predicate selectivity. Check each assumption before trusting a computed number.

PDF pp. 24–26

quiz.question: An equi-width bucket contains 4 values and 60 rows. What is the estimated equality count for one value?
quiz.explanation: Assuming uniformity within the bucket gives 60/4=15. This is an estimate based on equal frequencies, not the actual count if the data is skewed.
